clue.text: Usher in backers for Noel's singers

parts.note: to usher in something is to announce or herald its coming
theatrical backers who put up money for a show are called angels

explanation.surface: A theatre usher shows the show's financial backers to their seats at a Christmas carol concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text lost the U of 'Usher'; the printed page has it. 'Noel' here is Christmas, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hark the Herald Angels Sing is a carol; the phrase names the heavenly choir announcing the Nativity at Christmas.

clue.text: What to wear at home

parts.note: a habit is a garment, as a nun's or a riding habit

explanation.surface: A question of dress when staying indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text carries stray punctuation from the scan; 'at home' looks like one phrase, but 'at' gives AT and 'home' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitat is the natural dwelling place of an animal or plant, its living environment.

clue.text: Right way to accommodate ducks or hens here

indicators.note: the outer letters house or accommodate the inner pair

parts.note: ST, short for street, is a way
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, so two ducks are two zeros, OO

explanation.surface: A farmyard question of the right way to house ducks or hens.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a batter's score of zero, which is why ducks stand for a pair of round letters; 'to accommodate' puts them inside the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is the perch or place where hens settle to sleep.

clue.text: Agreeable OT country?

parts.note: a land in the Old Testament, east of Eden, imagined as a place where everyone nods assent

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some Old Testament nation was a pleasant one.
explanation.walkthrough: Cain was sent to this land in Genesis; a nod is a sign of agreement, so its people are 'agreeable'. It also means sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis names this place east of Eden where Cain dwelt; the phrase now also means the realm of sleep.

clue.text: She came to Siam with little money from India

explanation.surface: A woman travelled to Siam with only a small sum from India.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Leonowens was governess at the Siamese royal court, as in The King and I; also a small former coin of India, a sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Rags — some may be flimsy stuff

indicators.note: may be signals the letters of rags and some could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Some old rags might turn out to be fine filmy material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals rearranging the letters of RAGS SOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossamer is a fine, filmy fabric or cobweb, delicate and insubstantial.

clue.text: Put match to dynamite? Must be supple!

parts.note: to put a match to something is to light it, so lit
dynamite is a high explosive, abbreviated HE

explanation.surface: Lighting dynamite demands someone nimble enough to get away fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithe means bending easily and gracefully, flexible as a supple body is.

clue.text: Hermit sounds like a small holder in the main

indicators.note: the clue says the entry is heard as another word

parts.words: a small holder in the main
parts.note: an anchor holds a ship in the main, the sea; a little one would be an anchorette

explanation.surface: A recluse is said to resemble a smallholder, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small holder' suggests a smallholding farmer, but it is a little anchor, holding a ship in the main (the sea).
explanation.definitionFit: An anchoret, or anchorite, is a religious recluse who withdraws from the world.

clue.text: In agreement with many, made amends

parts.note: people at one are in agreement
D is the Roman numeral for 500, so many

explanation.surface: Agreeing with the majority, someone made up for a wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: To atone is to make reparation for a wrong, so the past tense means made up for it.

clue.text: Initiates, about to confess they're poets

indicators.note: one piece goes about, that is around, the other word

parts.note: to initiate a change is to bring it in or about, so brings
to own up is to confess, so own

explanation.surface: Novices in some order prepare to make their confession, revealing an artistic calling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiates' looks like a noun (newcomers) but is a verb; 'about' wraps it around the confession word. Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning were the married Victorian poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning, husband and wife, were both celebrated Victorian poets.

clue.text: A point in wine doctrine

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other word here

parts.note: tent is a deep red Spanish wine used for communion
a point of the compass, here east, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: Making a point about wine-drinking as a matter of belief.
explanation.walkthrough: TENT is an old name for a dark red Spanish wine, used in church; E, one compass point, goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief held as true by a group, which is what a doctrine is.

clue.text: Make lace also make designs

parts.note: to tat is to make lace by tatting, knotting thread by hand
too means also

explanation.surface: A craftsperson who does lacework and also decorative patterns.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattooing is marking designs into skin with ink and needles, so the verb means to make such designs.

clue.text: Grouse from a light-brown woman

parts.note: hazel is a light greenish-brown colour, as of hazelnuts
hen is an informal, chiefly Scottish, term for a woman

explanation.surface: Someone complains to a woman with hazel colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like a verb (complain) but is the game bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The hazel grouse is a woodland game bird of Europe, also called the hazel hen.

clue.text: Brings up suites

explanation.surface: Someone raises a matter about hotel rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: To train a child is to rear or bring it up; trains and suites are both retinues of attendants following a great person.

clue.text: A particular form of antipathy

parts.note: a version is a particular form of something

explanation.surface: Someone describes a specific kind of dislike.
explanation.definitionFit: Aversion is strong dislike, the same feeling of hostility antipathy names.

clue.text: With drink about of course must be restrained

indicators.note: the drink wraps about, that is around, the other word

parts.note: mead is a drink of fermented honey
sure, as a reply, means of course

explanation.surface: Someone drinking at a racecourse must keep themselves under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like part of a racing picture but is an affirmative reply; 'about' has the drink wrap around it, after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Measured speech or behaviour is deliberate and controlled, kept within bounds.

clue.text: Soaks brooded over acceptable local charges

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits over, above, the next

parts.note: a hen that brooded sat on its eggs
U means upper-class and so socially acceptable
rates were British local property taxes

explanation.surface: Drunks sat brooding over what council tax they would accept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soaks' looks like a noun (drunkards) but is the verb. Rates were Britain's local council taxes on property.
explanation.definitionFit: To saturate is to fill something with liquid until it can hold no more, as soaking does.

clue.text: Jack entertaining Jules Boniface

indicators.note: one word entertains, that is holds within it, the other

parts.note: jack and tar are both slang for a sailor
Jules Verne, the French science-fiction novelist

explanation.surface: A sailor plays host to a Frenchman named Jules, called Boniface.
explanation.walkthrough: Boniface, the landlord in Farquhar's play The Beaux' Stratagem, became a byword for an innkeeper; it is not a person here.
explanation.definitionFit: Boniface is a literary name for an innkeeper, and an old word for a pub keeper is the definition here.

clue.text: Great occasion for army exercise

explanation.surface: A big day for soldiers on manoeuvres.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically a highly enjoyable time or opportunity; originally a day of military manoeuvres and review in the open.

clue.text: Man of the match

explanation.surface: A player singled out as the best in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow is an informal word for a man or chap; it is also one of a pair, the counterpart that matches the other.

clue.text: Still gets first blow in — so

indicators.note: gets one piece placed in the other

parts.note: sic is Latin for so or thus, as used to flag a quoted error
tat is a light blow, as in tit for tat, blow for blow

explanation.surface: Someone stands motionless yet still manages to land the opening punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin 'so' is the word printed after a quoted mistake; 'in' puts the blow inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means motionless or unchanging, as still does as an adjective.

clue.text: Call round with dope — a freezing mixture

parts.note: to cry is to call out
O is round in shape
dope is slang for information, as is gen

explanation.surface: Ringing round with drugs to make a mixture that chills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' looks like a drug but means GEN, British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryogen is a substance used to produce very low temperatures, a refrigerant.

clue.text: One of those who heard de la Mare's traveller's call

definitions.text: One of those who heard de la Mare's traveller's call

parts.words: One of those who heard de la Mare's traveller's call
parts.note: in Walter de la Mare's poem, a Traveller knocks and calls at a moonlit house, heard only by a host of phantom hearers within

explanation.surface: A reader recalls the ghostly hearers in de la Mare's poem about a traveller knocking at a house.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text dropped the final word 'call'. The poem is The Listeners: 'Is there anybody there?' said the Traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: Each phantom in the poem is a hearer who attends silently to the Traveller's knocking and calling.

clue.text: To Antony, Caesar was a bleeding piece of it

definitions.text: To Antony, Caesar was a bleeding piece of it

parts.words: To Antony, Caesar was a bleeding piece of it
parts.note: Mark Antony, over the murdered body in Shakespeare's play, addresses it as a bleeding piece of soil or clay

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Antony mourning the stabbed body of Julius Caesar.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar III.i Antony says 'O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony calls the corpse a piece of soil or clay, the ground mortal bodies return to.

clue.text: Crafty, it ticklish

explanation.surface: A sly person, it seems, cannot bear being tickled.
explanation.definitionFit: Crafty as in cunning or sly; ticklish as in delicate and awkward to handle, as a problem can be.

clue.text: Cockney's companion honoured in a far eastern setting

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British honour
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Londoner's friend is decorated in an oriental setting.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so 'china' is a companion. 'far eastern setting' adds a second hint: the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang shortens china plate, rhyming with mate, to mean a friend.

clue.text: A stony-hearted girl friend?

parts.note: a sweetheart one goes out with, punningly also a fruit with a stone at its heart

explanation.surface: Asking whether a girlfriend is cold and unfeeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stony-hearted' suggests cruelty, but it is the stone at the centre of a palm fruit; a girlfriend is also someone you go out with.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit of a palm has a single stone at its centre, and a romantic partner one goes out with is also called this.

clue.text: Nothing grim, by repute

parts.note: O, the figure zero, stands for nothing
dour means grim and severe

explanation.surface: Nothing grim about one's reputation, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repute' is the definition through the idiom 'in good odour', meaning well thought of.
explanation.definitionFit: Odour can mean reputation or standing, as in being in good or bad odour with someone.

clue.text: The gin ran out — disaster just avoided

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the gin ran are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: The gin supply ran out, but catastrophe at the party was narrowly averted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' signals rearranging the letters of THE GIN RAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave or narrow escape, something that very nearly happened.

clue.text: Dickens lover in the "Plough"

parts.note: Charles is the first name of the novelist Dickens
a swain is a lover or suitor, especially a rustic one

explanation.surface: A romantic hero from a Dickens novel appears in a pub called the Plough.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plough is the British name for the seven-star group the US calls the Big Dipper.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for the seven bright stars of Ursa Major, known in Britain as the Plough.
